body.heading: A loop of string, a thousand pictures
paragraphs: A string figure begins with a loop of cord draped over the hands. With a choreography of fingers — under this loop, over that one, release and pull — the string rearranges into patterns: a cradle, a cup and saucer, a star, a running animal. Anthropologists have recorded string figures on every inhabited continent.

In many cultures the figures were storytelling props: an Inuit narrator might shape the characters of a tale as it unfolded, Pacific islanders wove long sequences to accompany chants, and the figures carried names, jokes and lessons with them.

body.heading: The two-player cradle
paragraphs: Cat's cradle is the famous two-player version. One player makes the cradle; the second pinches, lifts and transfers the string to transform it — cradle to candles, to the manger, to diamonds, and (if nobody fumbles) back again. Each transfer is a tiny act of trust: pull the wrong loop and the whole world collapses into spaghetti.

The collapse is part of the curriculum. String figures teach sequence, symmetry and patience, and they do it at the speed of fingers — which is why they survived every entertainment revolution since the Stone Age.

body.heading: Try it: learn the opening moves
paragraphs: Cut a metre of soft cord and tie the ends. Learn the cradle first (string behind both hands, pick up the far string with each middle finger), then teach a partner the first transfer. There are excellent slow diagrams in any string-games book; the fumbling is traditional and expected.
Graduation goal: the cup and saucer, a solo figure that ends with a satisfying reveal. Perform it for an audience of one grandparent and accept your applause.

takeaway: String figures are stories you hold in your hands — the oldest portable animation in the world.
